characters: Selinam: a 10-year-old girl in a school uniform with two puffs of hair, holding a notebook.
Rashid: her friend, 10, in a white shirt and brown shorts, who loves big animals.
Madam Lomotey: their teacher, in a green dress, holding a world map.
The yeti legend: a tall, shaggy, ape-like figure in snow far away, drawn as a story picture.
A Himalayan brown bear: a big shaggy brown bear in snow.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively storyteller voice; Madam Lomotey is warm and clear
narrationPlan.pace: Curious and lively, with a hush for the legend (about 115 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Cold wind, soft flute, a playful beat when the class investigates (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The Himalayas are on the other side of the world from Ghana. The pupils, school and teacher are invented. People in the Himalayas hold the yeti stories as part of their own culture, and the story treats them with respect.
Ghana has its own stories of forest creatures. Pupils may share them to compare how communities explain the unknown.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the DNA-study figures against the paper: Lindqvist et al., Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 2017 (nine “yeti” samples among 24 in total; mostly bears; one dog tooth).
Is the explanation of why bears might be mistaken for a yeti stated carefully as a possibility and not a certainty?

teacherGuide.overview: A “partly solved” mystery. It shows that science can answer one part of a story (what the tested samples were) while leaving other parts open.
learningGoals: Explain what evidence and DNA are in simple terms.
Separate what is solved from what is still unknown.
Show respect for stories and ask for proof.
beforeReading: Locate the Himalayas on a map. Ask: what stories do you know about forest creatures?
whileReading: At page 5, ask: does this solve everything?
afterReading: Make two lists, Solved and Not solved, for another legend.
Compare a yeti story with a Ghanaian forest story.
discussion: Why is it important to test samples?
Why do people keep telling the story?
reflection: What is a mystery you would like to solve?

mathsExtension.task: In the study, 9 samples were labelled “yeti”. If 8 were bears and 1 was a dog, what fraction were bears?

support: Provide a Solved / Not solved table with pictures.
stretch: Write a short report: “What the DNA can and cannot tell us.”

culturalNotes: The Himalayas are on the other side of the world from Ghana. The pupils, school and teacher are invented. People in the Himalayas hold the yeti stories as part of their own culture, and the story treats them with respect.
Ghana has its own stories of forest creatures. Pupils may share them to compare how communities explain the unknown.
localiseThis: Invite elders to share local forest stories and discuss how people explain things they cannot see.
Keep the tone respectful of every culture’s stories.

whatWeKnow: Nearly all the samples tested in the 2017 study came from bears, with one from a dog.
Bears can stand on two legs and leave large footprints.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: What every person who reported a yeti actually saw.
Whether any unknown large animal lives in the high mountains (there is no evidence so far).

factCheck.claim: A 2017 study by Charlotte Lindqvist’s team tested samples said to be yeti; they came from Himalayan and Tibetan brown bears and an Asian black bear, with one dog sample; the study linked legends to real bears.
factCheck.explanation: From National Geographic’s report. Sample counts differ in the article: nine “yeti” samples, 24 in all.
factCheck.reference: National Geographic, “Yeti legends: real animals, DNA, bears, Himalaya, science” (2017); original paper in Proceedings of the Royal Society B.
